# Markdown in, Markdown out {#chp:markdown}

Markdown is plain text, so generating it is mostly string work, as long as you
get the fences, pipes, and dollar signs right. The recipes here write
Markdown from R objects, and read it back without being fooled by code blocks.

## Turn a data frame into a table {#sec:md-table}

`md_table()` makes a pipe table, ready to paste into any Markdown document:

```{r}
md_table(head(mtcars[, 1:4], 3))
```

The result is a character vector, one line per element. Use `digits` and `na`
to tidy the cells, and `escape = TRUE` when the text contains Markdown
characters that should stay literal:

```{r}
df = data.frame(x = c(1.23456, NA), y = c('a|b', '<foo:bar>'))
md_table(df, digits = 2, na = 'n/a', escape = TRUE)
```

For long data, `limit = 10` keeps only the first and last rows and omits the
middle.

## Wrap content in a fenced block {#sec:fenced-block}

Code blocks and fenced Divs are just content between delimiter lines.
`fenced_block()` writes them, with optional attributes:

```{r}
fenced_block(c('x = 1', 'y = 2'), attrs = '.r')
```

Because the output starts with a blank line and the vector is easy to
`cat()`, it composes well with other text.

## Build a fenced Div {#sec:fenced-div}

A fenced Div uses colons instead of backticks. `fenced_div()` is shorthand for
`fenced_block(char = ':')`:

```{r}
fenced_div('Careful with this one.', attrs = c('.callout-warning', '#risk'))
```

## Pick a fence that cannot be broken {#sec:make-fence}

If your content already contains three backticks, a three-backtick fence ends
the block too early. `make_fence()` returns a fence one character longer than
the longest run in the content, and `fenced_block()` uses it automatically:

```{r}
x = c('```r', '1 + 1', '```')
make_fence(x)
fenced_block(x, attrs = '.md')
```

## Shield math from the Markdown parser {#sec:protect-math}

Underscores in `$a_1 + b_2$` can make Markdown italicize the text between them.
`protect_math()` wraps math in backticks so that the parser leaves it alone, and
you can restore it after rendering (the `token` argument marks the spots):

```{r}
protect_math('Inline $a_1 + b_2$ and display $$x_1^2$$ done.')
```

Inline math becomes `\(...\)` inside backticks, and display math keeps its
dollar signs.

## Find the prose lines in Markdown {#sec:prose-index}

A `#` inside a code block is not a heading. `prose_index()` returns the indices
of lines outside code fences, so you can search or rewrite only the text:

```{r}
x = c('Intro', '```r', '# a comment, not a heading', '```', 'The end')
i = prose_index(x)
i
x[i]
```

If the fences are unbalanced, all lines are treated as prose and you get a
warning.

## Convert R package news to Markdown {#sec:news2md}

`news2md()` reads a package's news through `news()` and writes it as Markdown,
with versions as first-level headers and categories as second-level ones. Set
`output = NA` to get the lines back instead of writing `NEWS.md`:

```{r}
head(news2md('R', output = NA), 4)
```

## Write a message to stdout {#sec:msg-cat}

`message()` goes to stderr, which is awkward when you capture stdout, as
knitr-style tools often do. `msg_cat()` writes to stdout but can still be
silenced by `suppressMessages()`. It does not add a newline for you:

```{r}
msg_cat('Working...\n')
suppressMessages(msg_cat('You will not see this.\n'))
```

## Control how values print when recording code {#sec:record-print}

`record()` runs code and keeps the output. For each visible value, it calls the
generic `record_print()`, so you can decide how your class shows up. Return a
`new_record()` with the content and its type:

```{r}
m = structure(3.5, class = 'money')
record_print.money = function(x, ...) {
  new_record(paste('USD', unclass(x)), 'output')
}
record('m')
```

Without the method, `m` would print through the normal `print()` output.
